This is the final lecture, and the content may not be as comprehensive as before, nor will it involve technical issues. It primarily introduces the operational process of North American projects. Below is the agenda:

First, an overview of relevant projects will be provided to give a general picture;

Next, business expansion methods will be explained, including project acquisition and market development;

Then, the bidding process and post-award project management will be discussed;

Finally, two typical cases will be analyzed—one that operated well and another that performed relatively poorly.

Next, we will focus on the scope of electrical engineering. These systems include but are not limited to:

Nurse call systems

Building automation systems

Energy control systems

Power systems

Fire alarm systems

Telecommunication systems

Elevator systems

Lighting systems

Closed-circuit television (CCTV) systems

Metering systems

Security systems

Nurse call systems  
Building automation systems  
Energy control systems  
Power systems  
Fire alarm systems  
Telecommunication systems  
Elevator systems  
Lighting systems  
Closed-circuit television (CCTV) systems  
Metering systems  
Security systems  
Intrusion detection systems  
Access control systems  
HVAC sensor systems  
Grounding/equipotential bonding/lightning protection systems  

These systems are listed here, and since everyone is relatively familiar with them, we will not elaborate further.  

From a professional perspective, executing a project typically involves the following processes:  
First, conduct a feasibility analysis, then proceed to the design phase, followed by tender and bidding activities, and finally commence construction. Although we are less involved in the specifics of the construction phase, post-project completion requires commissioning and concludes with close-out activities.

Project types span multiple sectors including industrial, commercial, and civil fields.

The project operation process is as follows: First, project opportunities need to be identified, which can be obtained through various channels, including personal referrals, public bidding (such as RFQ), and online bidding platforms. Nowadays, bidding is primarily conducted online, while traditional methods like newspaper announcements are rarely used.

During the bidding phase, a proposal must be prepared. Upon winning the bid, the project moves into the design and construction phases. This presentation primarily focuses on the construction phase, as the design aspect is already well-known. In North America, various permits are required before construction can begin. For example, a building permit serves as the general authorization for project commencement. Additionally, specialized permits are needed for various subcontracting trades, such as electrical, plumbing, and HVAC. Particularly for equipment like boilers, special permits are required in addition to the building permit.

Once all permits are approved, construction can commence. As the project nears completion, inspections are required, including those by engineering consultants and the Authority Having Jurisdiction (AHJ). Each permit corresponds to an independent AHJ inspection. For instance, the building permit is inspected by officials from the municipal building department (city development department or building permit department).

In terms of electrical work, the Electrical Safety Authority will dispatch an Electrical Inspector specifically to inspect and approve electrical installations. Typically, the Building Permit is handled by the Building Official, but their responsibilities may exceed capacity. The actual inspection is carried out by subordinate Subtrades.

The project involves multiple stakeholders, including clients, consultants (such as LWX Consultants), commissioning agents, and other key service departments. Additionally, there are other specialized subcontractors such as plumbing and HVAC contractors.

The project involves multiple stakeholders, including clients, consultants (such as LWX Consultants), commissioning agents, and other key service departments. Additionally, there are other specialized subcontractors such as plumbing and HVAC contractors.

For large-scale electrical contractors, a subcontracting model is typically adopted—for instance, after securing the main contract for both high-voltage and low-voltage electrical works, the low-voltage portion may be further subcontracted. As contractors, they must maintain close communication with suppliers (e.g., Hao Yuan Coordination), particularly during the procurement of materials and equipment, where frequent coordination between electrical contractors and suppliers is essential.

In the field of electrical engineering, project scales vary significantly, ranging from projects costing a few hundred yuan to large-scale projects worth billions. Typically, electrical engineering costs account for approximately 10% to 15% of the total project budget. In North America, electrical contractors are required to possess appropriate qualifications, including professional licenses. Each electrician must hold an individual license, which differs from the career path of engineers: engineers are considered white-collar professionals, whereas electrical contractors fall under the blue-collar skilled trades. The career progression for electricians includes different levels such as certified electricians and master electricians, all of which require obtaining corresponding licenses.

Only individuals holding a license or certified electrician qualifications can establish an electrical contracting company, similar to the requirements for design firms. Design firms need to have Professional Engineer (PE) certification and a business license, while electrical contracting companies also have specific qualification requirements. Throughout this process, project management and construction management are crucial.

Electrical contractors must comply with electrical codes and standards, though their familiarity with these regulations is generally less comprehensive than that of consulting firms. However, in terms of installation techniques, contractors often possess greater expertise. For instance, during electrical project inspections, officials primarily examine installation quality, and contractors may have a deeper understanding of inspection requirements than designers.

Next, we will explore issues related to market development.

Market development is primarily divided into several segments. The first is the Public Sector, which includes institutions such as governments, hospitals, and schools. Projects in this sector typically adopt an open bidding process, though not all companies are eligible to participate. The bidding process usually involves multiple rounds of screening. Initially, qualified bidders (Standing Offer) are identified through open tendering—these are pre-qualified consulting firms or contractors (Pre-qualified Consultant/Contractor). These companies are selected from a pool of bidders and are subsequently invited directly for future project bids.

Public sector tender information is usually published on specialized platforms, such as Merks.com in North America, which requires registration and an annual fee to access bidding details. Additionally, Canadian provinces and U.S. states have their own procurement websites for publishing engineering projects, procurement, and other service-based contracts.

As for the private sector, projects are typically handled through specific channels. Owners or developers may directly invite companies they deem suitable to bid or seek appropriate electrical consultants or electrical contractors through referrals or other means to undertake the projects.

Alternatively, you can directly approach the prime contractor. The design prime contractor is called the prime consultant, while the construction prime contractor is referred to as the GC (General Contractor), who then selects subcontractors independently.

Building a professional network is crucial in both private and public sectors. Market development requires self-promotion and company publicity, while potential opportunities are often gained through mutual understanding. Relying solely on online announcements yields limited results.

In the engineering and contracting industries abroad, especially in infrastructure design and construction, large-scale advertising is rarely used. Project opportunities are primarily obtained through industry channels and networks. Industry associations and organizations serve as key platforms for promoting individuals and companies.

From personal experience, initial recognition was gradually built through training and lectures, with high-quality service leading to client referrals. Friend recommendations and media advertisements accounted for a smaller share, while social media promotion is a different story.

In marketing within the engineering field, authority is the most critical factor. Due to the high barriers to entry in the industry—requiring licenses and professional expertise—projects demand strict authority. In North America, authority is the foremost factor in marketing engineering design consulting services.

Ways to establish authority include participating in industry organizations and association activities, hosting lectures, and showcasing company achievements and project cases on social media. Compared to traditional media advertising, professional promotion within the industry proves more effective.

In the B2B and B2C sectors, marketing strategies are entirely different. B2B clients purchase services rather than personal consumer goods. Especially in the consulting industry, the marketing approach has its unique characteristics.

In the B2B and B2C sectors, marketing strategies are entirely different. B2B clients purchase services rather than personal consumer goods. Especially in the consulting industry, the marketing approach has its unique characteristics.

Our target clients primarily include professionals such as property owners, developers, builders, general contractors, and engineers. For example, architects and other specialized engineers refer clients to us. As contractors, many general contractors seek us out as subcontractors for specialized trades, including electrical, plumbing, and HVAC. When they need an electrical contractor, they also recommend us. These are some of the ways we develop our market presence.

Next, I will explain how to secure projects.

First, the bid price must be competitive. However, the situation differs in the engineering design and consulting industry. In the private sector, developers typically prioritize pricing as their primary focus, given their profit-driven objectives. But in government projects, such as the Canadian government bids we participate in, the evaluation system employs a comprehensive scoring method where price accounts for only 10% of the total weight. The remaining 90% consists of approximately 20%-30% allocated to corporate qualifications, while 60%-70% evaluates team experience and technical expertise.

In addition to offering a competitive bid, it is essential to deliver high craftsmanship quality and service. Craftsmanship quality is reflected in the aesthetic and precision of project execution, while excellent service is equally indispensable. Furthermore, projects must be delivered on schedule and strictly within budget. Frequent change orders may lead to client attrition and jeopardize future collaboration opportunities.

Lastly, maintaining effective coordination and communication with all project stakeholders is crucial. This includes the client, design teams, and other involved parties to ensure smooth project progression.

Maintaining effective coordination and communication with all project stakeholders is crucial. This includes the client, design teams, and other involved parties to ensure smooth project progression.

When preparing bid documents, the appearance of the documents is crucial. Western culture places greater emphasis on superficial presentation, while Eastern culture prioritizes substantive content. Therefore, bids must be meticulously crafted. For large-scale projects, bid documents are particularly critical and may even require presentations. Even for small projects targeting mainstream white clients locally, submitting quotes on plain paper or via simple emails can appear unprofessional. This relates to the issue of professional image.

A company’s website and templates should be designed to be visually appealing and professional. Establishing a professional image and reputation through marketing is essential, falling under the scope of brand building. A strong brand image can generate follow-up business—we often encounter projects coming to us proactively, sometimes without even knowing who referred them. Many projects, from quoting to completion, are handled entirely via phone and email, and I’ve never even met the client in person.

When securing projects, understanding local conditions is key. Private business owners prioritize price, quality, and service, seeking cost savings and project safety without requiring bribes. In contrast, government and public sector clients in Western cultures do not engage in kickbacks, differing from Eastern practices. In the U.S. and Canada, strict regulations govern government employees’ acceptance of dinners, golf outings, or gifts—for example, U.S. rules prohibit accepting gifts worth over $25.

In business interactions, dining etiquette should be adapted to the context. For example, our company once participated in a bidding process for a commissioning project, where one of the evaluators was a council member reviewing our proposal team. I could host non-evaluating council members, but the evaluators insisted on paying for their own meals to maintain impartiality.

For government and public sector projects, the essential approach when dealing with specific personnel is to ensure flawless project execution and create tangible achievements through high-quality deliverables. Below, we will delve into specific strategies and methods for project bidding.

The specific process for bidding on a project is as follows: First, obtain project information and confirm eligibility to bid. Typically, the RFP (Request for Proposal) or RFQ (Request for Quotation/Qualification) is acquired through online channels or referrals. Prepare the bid documents according to the requirements.

Before submitting the bid, participation in a pre-bid meeting may be required. For renovation projects, a site visit is usually necessary, whereas for new construction projects, it may not be mandatory. Such meetings are sometimes compulsory, and failure to attend may disqualify the bidder.

After obtaining the tender documents, focus on the project schedule and scope of work, as these form the basis for the quotation. Clarify the work content, required costs, team configuration, and equipment needs. Additionally, confirm whether your qualification meets the requirements, including various certifications, insurance, and bond documents.

The tender documents will specify two key deadlines: the bid submission deadline and the question inquiry deadline. The client will provide unified responses to inquiries via an addendum after the inquiry deadline, clarifying project requirements and scope of work. Also, pay attention to safety and security requirements and other document specifications, which are considered paperwork during the bidding stage and differ from the requirements in subsequent construction or design phases.

Next is the section on tender requirements. This part specifies the detailed requirements for the tender in terms of format and content, typically divided into the technical section and the financial section. Government or public projects usually require both sections.

The technical section primarily includes the company profile, team introduction, past project experience, methodology or management approach, and how project completion will be ensured. The financial section covers pricing details, such as the total cost, hourly rates, change order procedures, and project-related expenses like travel costs, equipment purchases, and software tool acquisitions.

Within the technical section, reference project cases are particularly important. For example, if the current project involves office building construction, past projects of similar scale must be provided. Reference cases should include project scale, location, completion time, cost, as well as the contact person and details of the project owner for verification of authenticity and service quality.

Additionally, the tender format has specific requirements, especially for government projects. For instance, the project understanding section is limited to one page, individual resumes are capped at two pages per person, each reference case is restricted to one or two pages, and the entire tender has strict page limits.

Another key consideration is supplementary documents. After the tender documents are released, bidders may raise questions. The tendering authority will issue supplementary documents in response to these queries, and these documents also form part of the tender. Therefore, when preparing the tender, the content of supplementary documents must be taken into account.

When preparing bid documents, it is essential to thoroughly understand the content of the RFP/RFQ, as it constitutes a legally binding contract. The key lies in accurately grasping the client’s requirements and scope of work. Given that bid documents are often lengthy, experienced bidders prioritize reviewing critical sections while overlooking standardized template clauses. If there are any ambiguities in the tender documents, the bidder may request clarification from the client via email or designated channels regarding the scope of work, project requirements, or even apply for an extension of the bidding deadline.

The financial section is the core component of the bid, primarily comprising direct and indirect costs. Direct costs include labor, materials, and equipment expenses, while indirect costs refer to overheads such as human resources, marketing, and other expenditures not directly tied to the project, as well as routine expenses like travel.

After completing the above tasks, all supporting documents (e.g., qualification certificates, insurance proofs, etc.) must be consolidated to compile a comprehensive bid proposal. Typically, the proposal is drafted by the market or business development team, reviewed by company executives or project managers, and then submitted. The final submission should be a thoroughly proofread and finalized version of the bid proposal.

How to prepare a high-quality proposal, here are some practical tips.

How to prepare a high-quality proposal, here are some practical tips.

First, when preparing reference projects, it is essential to select a case that matches the scale, geographic location, and type of the target project as a benchmark. Second, a professional proposal template must be prepared. For bidding quotations, tools like the CHEN Estimation Manual or specialized software may be required to improve accuracy, which is critical for contracts. For consultants, Excel is usually sufficient for small projects but lacks precision for large-scale ones.

The proposal must clearly define the scope of work and specify how change orders will be handled if the original scope is exceeded. For example, if a project is scheduled for two years, additional costs for delays should be outlined to compensate for extra manpower, time, and effort.

Regarding pricing, the hourly rates in the market trends are generally competitive and relatively stable. Quotes should not be too low, as this may signal lack of confidence and risk losing the project, nor too high—typically, a middle-ground approach (excluding the highest and lowest bids) is adopted.

For large projects where experience is lacking, it is advisable to hire professional ASMeter or project managers for assistance. For Chinese immigrants or those with limited English proficiency, it is recommended to engage native English speakers from the outset to draft the bidding proposal—they are not only more efficient but also better versed in local thought processes and communication styles.

For individuals from the East or new immigrants, they may be unfamiliar with local conditions, leading to potential shortcomings in project preparation. During the bidding process, it is essential to comprehensively account for all costs and expenses. For instance, the previously mentioned commissioning and startup phases are often overlooked. Additionally, project delays can incur extra costs, which must also be factored in.

Generally speaking, the initial contract should be competitive, as much of the profit actually comes from subsequent change orders. For large-scale projects, legal counsel must be engaged to review the final quotation and tender documents, ensuring no legal issues exist. This involves liability and risk allocation, requiring legal intervention when necessary.

The above points cover market development and bidding. Next, we will briefly discuss the project execution process. After winning the bid, the contract must be signed, and implementation can commence upon completion of the signing.

This phase is called Client Mobilization. Next comes the Permit Application stage. It is important to note that the Building Permit is applied for by the Consultant during the design phase, while other Subtrade Permits (such as the Electrical Permit, etc.) are applied for by the Contractor during the construction phase. The Permit application process must be completed simultaneously with the commencement of on-site construction.

For Material Procurement, Shop Drawings must be submitted in advance for review by the Consultant, and procurement can only proceed after approval is obtained. During construction, strict compliance with local Electrical Codes and relevant regulatory standards is mandatory.

In terms of Construction Management, special attention should be paid to Project Management and the coordination work among various specialized subcontractors (Subtrade). Upon completion of all work, the project enters the Inspection Closeout phase, a process previously explained.

Regarding contract matters in large-scale projects, they typically involve formal contracts, which are usually prepared by lawyers and difficult to modify, especially those signed with government departments, as they are often mandatory.

In contrast, smaller projects can adopt simpler agreements with greater flexibility. Regardless of the type of contract, professionalism should be ensured to mitigate risks and liabilities.

At the project initiation stage, it is necessary to form a project team.

At the project initiation stage, it is necessary to form a project team.

This section involves specific operations, requiring preparation of materials, equipment, tools, as well as trailers, trucks, and warehousing, all of which are considerations during the construction process.

Additionally, when launching the project, arrangements must be made for accommodation and transportation, a project kickoff meeting should be held, a project schedule should be developed, and an on-site situation briefing should be conducted.

Safety aspects are particularly important, including safety training and daily safety management.

In terms of equipment procurement, different parties are responsible for different projects. For example, consumables such as wires and conduits are typically purchased by the contractors themselves, while large or critical equipment may be procured by the client and provided to the contractor for installation.

Equipment purchase orders must follow established approval procedures. The receipt and storage of materials and equipment after delivery must be properly arranged during the construction process.

A certain profit margin must be reserved during contract execution, and operational costs should be considered when quoting. Construction management encompasses cost control, budget management, scheduling, resource allocation, quality management, and change management.

Financial management includes invoice processing, expense reimbursement, and tax matters, while contract management involves the day-to-day operations of project-specific tasks.

For instance, when multiple subcontractors or suppliers are involved, effective management is still required. Additionally, coordination with consultants and the owner is crucial, including organizing construction meetings, preparing meeting minutes, and chairing meetings, all of which fall under the scope of contract management.

Matters such as change orders and progress payment applications are also included, making the content quite complex. As mentioned earlier, safety management is the top priority.

Regarding equipment inspection, if the equipment used has not been approved by local certification bodies in the United States or Canada, special certification is necessary.

Additionally, during the construction process, issues may be identified—for instance, during on-site inspections. If these problems were not detected during the design phase, there may be non-compliances with regulations. In such cases, a code adjustment is required, meaning an application for a variance must be filed.

During the closeout phase, a handover document package must be submitted, which includes as-built drawings.

During the closeout phase, a handover document package must be submitted, which includes as-built drawings. The online manual and the substantial completion certificate, these contents have been discussed previously. Of course, during demobilization, it is necessary to ensure the site is cleaned up and the warranty work is completed.

For electromechanical projects, a service contract can also be negotiated, such as an annual maintenance service contract for the fire protection system. If issues arise during project operation, temporary contact information should not be sought. Large-scale projects or systems usually require service contracts, especially for building automation systems, where such contracts are signed for nearly every project.

These contracts are typically signed by equipment manufacturers or system installers, adopting models such as hourly rates or annual fixed fees. This is how different project types operate, and industrial projects are no exception.

In large-scale industrial projects, the EPCM model is widely recognized. Additionally, there is the Design-Build model (integrated design and construction). The advantage of this model lies in the convenience of owner management and tighter coordination between design and construction. However, it poses challenges in quality control, as contractors may cut corners to save costs.

Another model is the P3 model (Public-Private Partnerships), commonly used for large municipal projects in North America. This model forms partnerships between private enterprises and public sectors, with private entities responsible for financing, construction, design, and long-term operation and maintenance. Governments leverage this approach to implement large municipal projects, alleviating fiscal pressure.

Furthermore, a common model involves separating consulting and construction, which is suitable for non-P3 projects. Under this model, consultants assist the owner in establishing engineering standards, with payment methods including Time and Material and Lump Sum.

Common types of contracts include Lump Sum Contracts, Time and Material Contracts, as well as bonus and penalty clauses based on project completion.

Common types of contracts include Lump Sum Contracts, Time and Material Contracts, as well as bonus and penalty clauses based on project completion.

Regarding qualification requirements:
- Developers do not require licenses in Canada.
- General Contractors (GCs) similarly need no licensing in Canada but must obtain qualifications in the U.S.
- Builders in Canada must secure relevant permits, though these are relatively easy to obtain.
- Contractors and various Trades must hold licenses, as previously explained.

For project management credentials:
- PMP Certification differs from engineering licenses—it is not legally mandatory but signifies the holder’s competency in project management. The certification process is straightforward.

Finally, two project examples are briefly mentioned, including the Enbridge Project, which I participated in (details covered earlier).

In the Alberta oil fields, the primary infrastructure consists of the pipeline transportation system. This system features large terminal stations at regular intervals, each equipped with multiple storage tanks. Crude oil is pressurized at pumping stations and transported through pipelines.

During my tenure as an electrical project lead, I participated in several major projects. Between 2012 and 2018, Enbridge invested CAD 28 billion in construction, with the projects I oversaw totaling approximately CAD 300–500 million. These projects were executed by experienced local teams.

The project began with a regional contract model valued at approximately CAD 200 million. It performed exceptionally well, with substantial time dedicated during the design phase to solution validation and feasibility studies, resulting in a change order rate below 5% during construction. The project remained within budget and on schedule throughout.

As a member of the owner’s project management team, I found Enbridge’s project management mechanisms and operational models to be industry benchmarks. Their professional project management processes left a strong impression and provided valuable insights for my subsequent entrepreneurial ventures.

Later, I participated in two oil terminal renovation projects in Vancouver. These projects involved upgrades to existing terminals acquired by Indonesian Chinese investors, whose management approach reflected Southeast Asian practices and differed significantly from North American standards.

As the overall lead for electrical and instrumentation engineering, I managed the entire process from design to construction. Although the contractors were highly skilled, the owner initiated bidding with only 60% design completion, leading to frequent changes later. The originally budgeted CAD 6 million for electrical and instrumentation work ultimately exceeded CAD 12 million, and the timeline extended to 24 months.

This approach starkly highlighted the differences in project management philosophies between Eastern and Western practices, primarily rooted in cultural and institutional contexts. These lessons warrant in-depth analysis.

The reason this company operates so well is that Enbridge hires local contractors who are familiar with the regional context, ensuring smooth collaboration. However, if China’s operational model or an Asian approach were applied to Canadian projects, it would be difficult to manage contracts effectively, resulting in high costs and hard-learned lessons.

That said, everything has two sides—challenges and opportunities coexist. By summarizing experiences, one can learn and improve project management capabilities. Currently, Chinese companies still face numerous challenges when operating projects in Canada or other countries.

In recent years, it has become increasingly common for Chinese companies to conduct business in Africa. Just yesterday, I assisted a Chinese company with a project in Canada. After the meeting concludes, I can share relevant experiences with everyone.

Next, we will address these two questions.

First, regarding the lighting control issue, I will explain through a sketched diagram. The lighting control panel is typically divided into a circuit breaker panel and a contactor panel. For example, this is the circuit breaker panel, next to it is the contactor panel, and below them are connected luminaires, forming a lighting circuit.

The power supply for the contactor coil is achieved through two dry contacts. One dry contact is a parallel-connected push-button switch, and the other comes from the Building Management System (BMS). Under normal conditions, the circuit is energized. When the button is pressed, the normally open contact closes, forming a circuit, the contactor coil is energized, the contacts close, and the luminaires light up.

A single contactor can be equipped with multiple normally open and normally closed contacts. For instance, four normally open contacts can control four lighting circuits. If there are 20 circuits in the panel, five contactors are required. When the button is released, the circuit is de-energized, the contacts open, and the luminaires turn off.

If BMS control is used, the signal is sent by the BMS, and control is achieved through the normally open contact.

The system features a built-in clock function that enables automatic light control through time settings. For instance, the signal closes at 7:00 AM to turn on the lights, and opens at 6:00 PM to turn them off. The circuit diagram is simplified; in practice, mode switching can also be achieved via a manual/automatic transfer switch (H-Always switch).

The basic circuit consists of a breaker panel and a contact panel, suitable for simple control scenarios. For theater lighting systems, a more sophisticated lighting control panel is required. Power is supplied from the breaker panel, processed by the lighting control panel, and then distributed to individual circuits.

OK, next question: The front end of mechanical equipment needs to be equipped with an isolation switch to cut off the power supply during maintenance. What are the specific regulatory requirements for this part?

The specification has clear requirements, especially for electric motors. For instance, when a large number of air conditioning units are installed outdoors or on rooftops, and the switches and distribution boxes are located indoors, accidents can easily occur if someone mistakenly operates the switch to restore power during maintenance above. Therefore, local isolation switches must be installed. No matter how the lower section is operated, as long as this switch is turned off, even if power is restored below, it will not cause issues.

For the commissioning of large systems, the situation is more complex. Each device should be equipped with a local isolation switch and a locking mechanism. The person in charge of commissioning or startup will carry a dedicated key. When working on lower-end equipment, they will go to the MCC or other locations to disconnect the power and lock it, while also hanging a “Lockout Tag” sign. No one is allowed to operate the device without authorization. This method applies to the startup and commissioning phases, while during the installation and design phases, configurations must be made according to the device’s power requirements.

Small appliances like lighting equipment only require ordinary switches, but general equipment, especially motors, must have isolation switches. In addition to the risk of electric shock, motors also pose mechanical hazards, such as long hair getting caught in exposed motors, which can lead to serious injuries or fatalities. Canadian motor regulations stipulate that if the distribution panel is indoors and the distance exceeds 9 meters, isolation switches may be omitted if the panel is visible and power can be cut off promptly. Otherwise, they must be installed. This requirement primarily targets motors, but devices with motors in air conditioning systems, such as fans and compressors, must also comply. Other equipment similarly requires appropriate protective measures.

Teacher Fan, I’d like to add a point regarding this issue.

Regarding the discussion on motor disconnect switches, as I mentioned to you in the email, we need to conduct an in-depth study of specific codes and standards.  

In our daily work, when communicating technical issues with Jianmin, the most compelling way to present arguments is by referencing U.S. standards and codes. We are willing to review U.S. standards line by line and provide technical interpretations and learning for each clause.  

As you pointed out, certain requirements do exist in U.S. standards, but the key lies in identifying the specific source—which standard’s exact clause it is. This is the critical task we need to follow up on, rather than remaining at vague statements like “the standard requires it.”

Next, I will continue discussing the content previously communicated via email. We aim to conduct an in-depth study of critical components in electrical systems, such as fire protection systems and integrated control systems, along with the U.S. code basis for relevant calculation parameters. For instance, regarding generator startup time requirements, domestic designers can typically quickly reference values from local standards (e.g., 10, 15, or 30 seconds). We hope to extend this rapid referencing capability to the U.S. code system, ensuring immediate identification of specific standard clauses when questions arise.

The distinction between NEC and NFPA should be clarified first. The NEC is a code and also a standard within the NFPA framework. NFPA (National Fire Protection Association) is an organization that develops numerous standards. Within the NFPA system, the NEC is designated as NFPA 70, while the fire alarm system standard is NFPA 72. Countries such as the United States and Canada have similar organizational structures and standard systems. For example, in the U.S., there are overlapping relationships between NFPA and NC standards, and Canada follows a similar pattern, where its CEC standard corresponds to Part 20.1 of CSA.

These standard systems cover a wide range of areas, not limited to electrical fields. Electrical standards and fire alarm system standards are just components of them. At the beginning of the course, the overall framework of these standard systems was emphasized to help establish a foundational understanding. This includes the standards and codes involved in electrical design, the institutions that develop them, the authority of interpretation, and their implementation methods.

Regarding the systematic organization of these codes and standards, this will be a key focus of my future work. After completing the explanation of electrical design guidelines, I will systematically compile relevant content such as building codes, electrical codes, and fire alarm system codes. I plan to provide a detailed interpretation of electrical code standards in North America. For instance, Canada’s electrical code is very comprehensive, while China’s electrical code is relatively concise by comparison. Taking the 2008 edition as an example, the electrical section was only 120 pages long, mostly consisting of principle-based guidelines with few detailed implementation rules. In contrast, standards like the NEC typically span five to six hundred pages with exhaustive details.

This is precisely the core we aim to investigate—not only understanding what but also why. Within the Chinese regulatory system, there exists a widespread consensus: it functions more like a quick-design reference manual. Users only need to know specific parameter requirements (e.g., room illuminance must reach 100 lux) without grasping the derivation process or theoretical foundations behind these values. This characteristic of “emphasizing outcomes over process” precisely reflects both the strengths and limitations of China’s regulatory framework.

According to the 2008 edition of the code, upon review, the content involved is relatively brief. For example, regarding the fire alarm system, the code references the NIPA 72 standard; while for the security technology protection (Security) section, as well as systems such as broadcasting, conferencing, and cable television, the code’s provisions and explanations are quite concise. In comparison, the relevant North American codes are more detailed.

I can provide a code interpretation for these contents. If you have any specific systems or aspects of particular concern, please let me know, and I will focus on interpreting those.
